title: Major Depression: Diagnose Beyond the PHQ-9
bottomLine: Screening identifies possible depression; the clinical interview establishes the diagnosis, severity, suicide risk, bipolarity and medical/substance contributors. Before starting an antidepressant, ask about prior mania/hypomania and mixed symptoms.
recognize: Persistent low mood or loss of interest plus cognitive, sleep, appetite, psychomotor, energy, guilt/worthlessness and concentration symptoms with functional impairment support MDD.
Irritability may predominate in adolescents; older adults may present with somatic/cognitive concerns.
Peripartum depression requires the same safety assessment plus infant/caregiver functioning and postpartum psychosis screening.
differentiate: Bipolar depression is suggested by prior mania/hypomania, antidepressant-induced activation, episodic course, decreased need for sleep and family history.
Grief can coexist with MDD; bereavement does not exclude depression.
Thyroid disease, anemia, sleep disorders, medications and substance use can mimic or worsen depressive symptoms.
assessment: Assess duration, impairment, prior episodes/treatment, mania/hypomania, psychosis, substance use, trauma, anxiety and suicide/self-harm risk.
Review pregnancy/lactation, medical comorbidity and medication contributors.
workup: Use validated scales to measure severity/change, not as a stand-alone diagnosis.
Order medical tests only when symptoms/history suggest a contributor rather than using a universal 'depression panel'.
management: Use shared decision-making among psychotherapy, pharmacotherapy and combined care according to severity, preference, access and past response.
CANMAT 2023 provides evidence-based medication and psychotherapy options and emphasizes measurement-based follow-up.
Psychotic depression, catatonia, severe functional collapse or imminent suicide risk requires urgent specialty/acute-care management.
medicationSafety: Discuss early adverse effects, activation, sexual effects, discontinuation symptoms and expected time course.
Monitor for emerging mania/mixed symptoms after antidepressant initiation.
Pregnancy/lactation decisions should weigh untreated illness risk against medication risk rather than reflexively stopping effective therapy.
redFlags: Severe inability to eat/drink/care for self or infant
counselling: Set a concrete follow-up date and normalize treatment adjustment if the first intervention is insufficient.
Use behavioural activation/sleep/activity goals as adjuncts without implying depression is a willpower problem.
followUp: Reassess symptoms, function, adverse effects, adherence and suicide risk after initiation/change; continue effective treatment long enough to reduce relapse risk.
examTrap: Starting an SSRI after a positive screening score without asking about previous mania/hypomania or current suicide risk.
oneLinePearl: Depression treatment starts with two exclusions: immediate danger and bipolarity.
sourceBasis: CANMAT 2023 Update on Major Depressive Disorder

title: Mania and Bipolar Disorder
bottomLine: Mania is not 'feeling energetic': it is a sustained pathologic change in mood/energy with impaired judgment and function, often requiring urgent containment. Do not treat bipolar depression as unipolar depression without a mood-stabilizing strategy.
recognize: Decreased need for sleep, pressured speech, racing thoughts, grandiosity, increased goal-directed activity, distractibility and risky behaviour are classic manic features.
Severe mania can include psychosis, agitation, aggression, dehydration/exhaustion or financial/sexual/legal harm.
Postpartum mania/psychosis can emerge rapidly and is a psychiatric emergency.
differentiate: Substance/stimulant intoxication, corticosteroids, hyperthyroidism and neurologic disease can cause manic-like states.
ADHD is chronic and developmentally persistent; mania is episodic change from baseline with altered sleep/energy/mood.
assessment: Assess sleep, spending/risk behaviour, psychosis, agitation, suicide risk, violence risk, substance use and ability to care for self/dependents.
Obtain collateral information when safe/appropriate because insight may be impaired.
workup: Use targeted medical/toxicology testing for first episode, atypical age or suspected secondary cause.
Pregnancy testing and metabolic/renal/thyroid baseline testing may be needed depending on medication choice.
management: Severe mania, psychosis or unsafe behaviour requires urgent psychiatric assessment and often hospital-level care.
Use evidence-based mood stabilizer/atypical antipsychotic treatment matched to episode and patient factors; psychotherapy and relapse planning matter after stabilization.
For bipolar depression, choose treatments supported for bipolar disorder rather than antidepressant monotherapy.
medicationSafety: Lithium requires renal/thyroid monitoring, hydration consistency, interaction review and toxicity counselling.
Valproate has major reproductive/teratogenic concerns and requires strict pregnancy-risk consideration.
Antipsychotics require metabolic and movement-disorder monitoring.
redFlags: No sleep for days with escalating behaviour
counselling: Teach early relapse signs—especially reduced need for sleep—and involve supports with consent when feasible.
followUp: Monitor mood switching, sleep, medication toxicity/metabolic effects and adherence; ensure rapid access if activation recurs.
examTrap: Prescribing antidepressant monotherapy to a patient with a clear history of mania because the current visit looks depressive.
oneLinePearl: Ask about decreased need for sleep before calling depression unipolar.

title: Anxiety and Panic: Rule Out the Body First
bottomLine: Panic is a clinical diagnosis after the presentation fits and dangerous medical mimics are reasonably excluded. Long-term anxiety treatment relies on psychotherapy and appropriate maintenance pharmacotherapy—not repeated benzodiazepine rescue.
recognize: Panic attacks peak rapidly with fear plus autonomic/cognitive symptoms such as palpitations, dyspnea, chest tightness, tremor, dizziness or fear of dying/losing control.
Panic disorder requires recurrent unexpected attacks plus ongoing concern/behaviour change.
differentiate: ACS, arrhythmia, PE, asthma, hypoglycemia, hyperthyroidism, stimulant/caffeine intoxication and withdrawal can mimic anxiety/panic.
GAD is persistent excessive worry across domains rather than discrete abrupt attacks.
assessment: For a first/atypical attack, assess vitals, cardiac/respiratory symptoms, substance use, medications and medical risks.
Assess depression, suicide risk, trauma, OCD and substance use because comorbidity is common.
workup: Use targeted ECG/glucose/thyroid or other testing based on clinical risk; avoid repetitive extensive workups once a stable documented pattern is established and no new red flags exist.
management: CBT/exposure-based psychotherapy is high-value first-line care; SSRIs/SNRIs and other evidence-based options are used according to disorder and preference.
Teach paced breathing/grounding as short-term coping, but do not present them as substitutes for definitive treatment.
Reserve benzodiazepines for narrow short-term indications because dependence, falls and interaction risk can outweigh benefit.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines plus opioids/alcohol substantially increase sedation/overdose risk.
SSRIs/SNRIs can transiently increase activation early; start/titrate appropriately and monitor younger/high-risk patients.
counselling: Explain the physiologic panic cycle without dismissing symptoms as imaginary.
Encourage gradual exposure rather than broad avoidance that reinforces the disorder.
followUp: Track function/avoidance and frequency of attacks, not only symptom score; reassess diagnosis if the pattern changes.
examTrap: Calling a first episode of chest pain, tachycardia and dyspnea a panic attack before assessing medical causes.
oneLinePearl: Panic is real physiology—but first episodes still earn a medical differential.

title: First-Episode Psychosis
bottomLine: New psychosis is a syndrome, not automatically schizophrenia. Establish safety, rule out delirium/substance/medical causes, identify postpartum or neurologic emergencies, then connect the patient rapidly with early-psychosis/psychiatric care.
recognize: Delusions, hallucinations, disorganization, negative symptoms and functional decline can reflect primary psychosis.
Visual hallucinations, fluctuating attention, abnormal vitals or abrupt onset increase concern for delirium/toxic/neurologic causes.
Postpartum psychosis often includes severe mood symptoms, insomnia, confusion, delusions or bizarre behaviour and places parent/infant at acute risk.
differentiate: Delirium has impaired attention/awareness with acute fluctuation and medical cause until proven otherwise.
Substance-induced psychosis follows intoxication/withdrawal timing; primary psychotic illness requires longitudinal assessment.
Mania/depression with psychotic features is mood-linked rather than automatically schizophrenia.
assessment: Assess suicide/violence risk, command hallucinations, ability to care for self, access to weapons/means, substance use and medical symptoms.
Perform mental status plus neurologic/physical examination and seek collateral information when appropriate.
workup: Use glucose, CBC/electrolytes, toxicology, pregnancy, thyroid, infection/neurologic testing and imaging selectively according to age/onset/clinical clues.
management: Unsafe/agitated/medically abnormal patients need urgent emergency assessment.
Use antipsychotic treatment when primary psychosis is likely, selecting medication collaboratively and monitoring metabolic/neurologic effects.
Early-intervention services improve continuity for first-episode psychosis; arrange rapid follow-up, not a distant routine referral.
medicationSafety: Monitor weight/metabolic parameters, QT risk where relevant, movement disorders and hyperprolactinemia according to agent.
Avoid escalating sedatives before addressing delirium/intoxication/withdrawal and environmental de-escalation.
counselling: Use non-confrontational language: acknowledge distress without validating delusional content.
Include family/supports with consent and discuss relapse signs/sleep/substance risk.
followUp: Ensure metabolic monitoring, adherence/tolerability review and early-psychosis/psychiatric follow-up.
examTrap: Diagnosing schizophrenia in an older adult with abrupt visual hallucinations and fluctuating attention before evaluating delirium/medical causes.
oneLinePearl: First psychosis: safety, delirium/substances/medical causes, then primary psychiatric diagnosis.

title: Suicide Risk: Ask Directly, Plan Specifically
bottomLine: Suicide assessment is not prediction. Ask directly about thoughts, plan, intent, access to means, recent behaviour, dynamic stressors and protective factors, then choose a level of care that can actually maintain safety and build a collaborative safety plan.
recognize: Risk increases with prior attempts, current intent/plan/means, escalating hopelessness/agitation, substance use, psychosis, severe insomnia, recent loss and transition/discharge periods.
A patient may deny suicidal thoughts despite high concern; collateral information and observed behaviour can matter.
differentiate: Passive death wishes are not identical to active intent but still require assessment of progression, means and protective factors.
A numerical risk score cannot replace clinical assessment or justify discharge by itself.
assessment: Ask directly and nonjudgmentally about ideation, plan, intent, rehearsal/preparatory acts, access to means and prior attempts.
Assess intoxication, psychosis, impulsivity, supports, housing, children/dependents and ability/willingness to use a safety plan.
workup: Medical/toxicology evaluation is indicated when overdose, intoxication, delirium, self-injury or other medical cause is possible.
management: Imminent risk or inability to maintain safety requires emergency psychiatric/medical assessment and a secure environment.

For appropriate outpatient management, create a collaborative written safety plan: warning signs, internal coping, people/places for distraction/support, professional contacts and lethal-means reduction.
Treat the underlying disorder and substance use while actively managing short-term risk.
medicationSafety: When overdose risk is significant, consider toxicity and quantity dispensed; coordinate medication access safely rather than withholding all treatment.
Avoid sedative combinations that increase disinhibition/overdose risk.
redFlags: Current intent with access to lethal means
counselling: Asking about suicide does not create suicidal thoughts; direct questions improve clarity.
Involve trusted supports with consent when safe; privacy can be overridden according to law/policy when necessary to prevent serious imminent harm.
followUp: Arrange rapid proactive follow-up after crises/transitions and confirm the patient can access the plan; document the reasoning, not just 'contracts for safety'.
examTrap: Using a 'no-suicide contract' or low screening score as the main reason to discharge a patient with a specific plan and accessible means.
oneLinePearl: Risk assessment asks what could happen next; safety planning specifies what happens instead.
sourceBasis: CAMH Suicide Risk Assessment and Prevention Resources

title: Opioid Use Disorder and Overdose Prevention
bottomLine: OUD is a treatable chronic health condition. Canadian CRISM guidance recommends buprenorphine and methadone as standard first-line opioid agonist treatments; withdrawal management alone increases relapse and mortality and should not be the treatment plan.
recognize: Loss of control, craving, hazardous use, continued use despite harm, role impairment, tolerance and withdrawal contribute to OUD diagnosis.
Fentanyl exposure increases overdose risk and can complicate buprenorphine initiation strategies.
Pregnancy with OUD requires prompt evidence-based treatment, not forced withdrawal.
differentiate: Tolerance/physical dependence from prescribed opioids does not by itself equal OUD.
Acute opioid overdose presents with depressed consciousness/respiration and often miosis; mixed overdoses can alter the picture.
assessment: Assess overdose history, current opioid/fentanyl exposure, route, other sedatives/alcohol, withdrawal, pregnancy, infection risk, pain, mental health, housing and treatment goals.
Use non-stigmatizing language and ask what has worked before.
workup: Testing for infections, pregnancy, ECG or labs depends on chosen therapy and risk; drug testing should support care rather than punish the patient.
management: Offer buprenorphine or methadone as first-line OAT; slow-release oral morphine is a second-line option in the national guideline.
Do not require counselling participation as a condition for access to OAT.
Provide take-home naloxone, overdose education, safer-use supplies/referral and infection prevention.
Overdose: airway/ventilation support and naloxone with emergency response; recurrence can occur after naloxone wears off.
medicationSafety: Concurrent benzodiazepines/alcohol increase overdose risk but should prompt careful management—not automatic denial of OAT.
Methadone initiation has higher early mortality risk than later treatment and requires careful dosing/monitoring; buprenorphine initiation can precipitate withdrawal if timed incorrectly.
redFlags: Loss of tolerance after abstinence/release from custody
counselling: Teach naloxone to the patient/supports, reduced tolerance after abstinence and risks of using alone or combining sedatives.
followUp: Keep treatment accessible after return to use; retention in OAT is a major safety outcome.
examTrap: Offering detoxification alone or requiring psychotherapy before prescribing opioid agonist therapy.
oneLinePearl: For OUD, retention in evidence-based treatment saves lives; detox alone does not.
sourceBasis: CRISM National Guideline for the Clinical Management of Opioid Use Disorder 2024

title: Alcohol Withdrawal and Alcohol Use Disorder
bottomLine: Separate acute withdrawal risk from long-term AUD treatment. Severe/complicated withdrawal is a medical emergency treated with benzodiazepine-based protocols and thiamine/supportive care; after stabilization, offer evidence-based AUD medication and psychosocial support rather than stopping at detox.
recognize: Withdrawal can begin within hours after reduced alcohol intake; tremor, autonomic activation, anxiety, nausea and insomnia can progress to seizures or delirium tremens.
History of withdrawal seizures/DTs, very heavy sustained use, older age, significant medical disease or concurrent sedative withdrawal increases risk.
differentiate: Alcohol intoxication can coexist with withdrawal risk later.
Delirium tremens includes delirium plus severe autonomic hyperactivity and requires hospital care; uncomplicated tremor/anxiety is not the same severity.
CIWA-Ar is a monitoring tool for appropriate patients, not a substitute for clinical judgment in delirium/noncommunicative patients.
assessment: Clarify last drink, typical quantity, prior severe withdrawal, other sedatives, seizures, pregnancy, liver disease, nutrition and current vitals/mental status.
Screen for AUD severity and treatment goals after the acute phase.
workup: Check glucose/electrolytes, CBC/liver tests and other investigations according to severity and comorbidity; evaluate alternate delirium causes.
management: Use benzodiazepine-based withdrawal treatment according to risk/protocol; severe withdrawal/DTs/seizures require acute-care management.
Give thiamine in patients at risk of deficiency and correct fluids/electrolytes/nutrition safely.
For moderate/severe AUD, medications such as naltrexone or acamprosate should be offered when appropriate even if the patient is not engaging in formal psychosocial treatment.
medicationSafety: Naltrexone is inappropriate with current opioid use/dependence and requires hepatic assessment; acamprosate requires renal consideration.
Benzodiazepine prescribing beyond the withdrawal window can create new dependence/sedation risk.
counselling: Use nonjudgmental discussion of goals including abstinence or reduced harm; offer pharmacotherapy and supports rather than insisting on one pathway.
followUp: Ensure transition from withdrawal care to ongoing AUD treatment; reassess craving, alcohol use, liver/medical health and medication response.
examTrap: Completing a 3-day withdrawal protocol and discharging without offering medication/treatment for the underlying alcohol use disorder.
oneLinePearl: Detox treats withdrawal; it does not treat AUD.
sourceBasis: Canadian Guideline for Clinical Management of High-Risk Drinking and AUD 2023
CAMH Alcohol Withdrawal and AUD Pharmacotherapy Resources

title: Eating Disorders: Medical Instability Can Hide
bottomLine: Eating disorders occur at any body size. Assess medical instability—bradycardia, hypotension/orthostasis, hypothermia, electrolyte/ECG abnormalities, dehydration and rapid weight loss—rather than using appearance or BMI as the gatekeeper for seriousness.
recognize: Restriction, binge eating, compensatory vomiting/laxatives/exercise, intense weight/shape concern, amenorrhea/endocrine change or rapid weight trajectory can signal an eating disorder.
Atypical anorexia can produce severe malnutrition/instability at a 'normal' or high BMI.
differentiate: Avoid assuming GI/endocrine symptoms are psychiatric without appropriate medical evaluation.
ARFID is driven by sensory/aversive/low-interest factors rather than weight/shape concerns.
assessment: Ask directly about eating pattern, restriction, bingeing, vomiting, laxatives/diuretics, compulsive exercise, weight trajectory, syncope, chest symptoms and suicide/self-harm.
Check lying/standing vitals, temperature and signs of dehydration/malnutrition.
workup: Electrolytes, glucose, renal function, magnesium/phosphate and ECG are important when purging, significant restriction, rapid loss or instability is present; additional tests are cause-directed.
management: Medical instability requires urgent specialized/hospital assessment.
Use evidence-based multidisciplinary care and family-based treatment for many adolescents; do not recommend dieting/weight loss while an active restrictive disorder is being treated.
Refeeding high-risk malnutrition requires monitoring for electrolyte shifts.
medicationSafety: QT-prolonging drugs and medications lowering seizure threshold require extra caution in electrolyte disturbance/malnutrition.
Bupropion is contraindicated in bulimia/anorexia because of seizure risk.
counselling: Use weight-neutral, non-shaming language and focus on nutrition/medical recovery and function.
Include caregivers/supports appropriately, especially for youth.
followUp: Track vitals, weight trajectory, labs when indicated, eating behaviours and psychiatric safety; coordinate specialty care.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because BMI is not low despite rapid weight loss, bradycardia and restrictive intake.
oneLinePearl: Medical severity is physiology, not appearance.
